Salt marsh

A salt marsh is a coastal ecosystem in the upper intertidal zone, flooded and drained by salt water brought in by the tides.[1] It is dominated by dense stands of salt-tolerant plants such as herbs, grasses and low shrubs, which have adapted to regular submergence.[2]

Salt marshes are among the most biologically productive habitats on the planet, and a single hectare can hold more than 106 individual invertebrates in its upper sediment layer.[citation needed]

Formation

[edit]

Sediment supply

[edit]

Marshes form where fine sediment settles out of slack water faster than currents can carry it away. Over decades the deposit rises high enough that pioneer plants can root, and the plants then trap more sediment, accelerating the process.3

The rate of accretion is what decides whether a marsh can keep pace with rising sea level. Where sediment is plentiful a marsh can climb by several millimetres a year, which is enough to survive moderate rises in the level of the sea.

Vegetation zones

[edit]

Plants sort themselves into bands by how long they can tolerate being underwater. The lowest band floods twice a day, while the highest is reached only by the spring tides, and the species in each are almost entirely different from one another.
